sentences.text: Ichthyornis is an extinct genus of toothed, seabird-like ornithuran named for its fish-like vertebrae. Its name means "fish-bird" because the bones in its spine resemble those found in fish. It is notable for having concave vertebrae in both the front and rear sections, a feature similar to that of some fish.

This bird had teeth only in the middle of its jaws, while the tips were toothless and covered by a beak. An average Ichthyornis specimen was about 24 cm long with a skeletal wingspan of approximately 43 cm.

The genus Ichthyornis was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1872. Ichthyornis was discovered in 1870 by Benjamin Franklin Mudge in the North Fork of the Solomon River in Kansas. Benjamin Franklin Mudge recovered fossils from the Solomon River in Kansas, USA.
A full re-description of Ichthyornis specimens was published by paleontologist Julia Clarke in 2004.

Ichthyornis is thought to have been the Cretaceous equivalent of modern seabirds like gulls, petrels, and skimmers. Ichthyornis is thought to have been the ecological equivalent of modern seabirds like gulls, petrels, and shearwaters during the Cretaceous.

Studies of Ichthyornis brain casts show it had a relatively basal brain similar to Archaeopteryx and non-avian theropods. Ichthyornis had a palate that was remarkably similar to that of modern neognath birds.
Ichthyornis specimens from earlier eras were generally smaller than those from later periods.

Marsh classified Ichthyornis in the new subclass Odontornithes and order Ichthyornithes due to its unique concave vertebrae and teeth. Due to its unique features like concave vertebrae on both sides and teeth, Marsh classified the bird into its own subclass called Odontornithes, meaning "toothed birds," and the new order Ichthyornithes (later Ichthyornithiformes). The genus Ichthyornis was originally placed in the subclass Odontotormae by Marsh in 1875.

In Julia Clarke's 2004 review, the former order Ichthyornithiformes and family Ichthyornithidae were superseded by the clade Ichthyornithes. Ichthyornis is close to the ancestors of modern birds, the Neornithes, but represents an independent lineage. The genus Ichthyornis belongs to the parent group Ichthyornithes.

Earlier Ichthyornis remains date to the early Turonian (about 93 million years ago) in Kansas and the late Cenomanian in Saskatchewan. Ichthyornis lived in North America between 93 and 75 million years ago. Older fossils attributed to Ichthyornis have been found in the Greenhorn Formation of Kansas dating to the early Turonian (about 93 million years ago) and in Saskatchewan dating to the Cenomanian (about 95 million years ago). Ichthyornis lived from the Cenomanian to the Campanian stages, between 100.5 and 72.2 million years ago.
Fossils of Ichthyornis are found in the Western Interior Seaway deposits across Alberta, Alabama, Kansas, New Mexico, Saskatchewan, and Texas.
